analysis.title: Energy Fuels - Government funding comes through for Donald
key_insights: Export Finance Australia and the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation conditionally approved up to A$180M (US$126M) for Phase 1 of the Donald Rare Earth and Mineral Sands project in Australia. The facility is still subject to due diligence and final approvals.
Canaccord calls the news positive. The debt package solves for most of the remaining funding needed to reach a final investment decision (FID) on Donald.

Donald is a fully permitted JV with Astron Limited, with Energy Fuels earning in to 49%. It is a key upstream component of EFR's mine-to-magnet supply chain and will supply rare earth mineral feedstock to the White Mesa mill in Utah.

The A$180M is part of a proposed A$200M senior project finance debt facility: up to A$70M from EFA, A$110M from NRF, and the remaining A$20M from commercial lenders. The government tranches have a 10-year tenor and are priced at BBSY plus a margin.
Debt proceeds cover construction, commissioning, financing and ramp-up costs at Donald.
FID for Donald is now expected before year-end 2026, a delay from the previous Q3 2026 timing. The construction window is expected to be 23 months.

Phase 1 is expected to produce about 9,000tpa of rare earth concentrate and 225,000tpa of heavy mineral concentrate (zircon and titanium minerals). EFR will buy all the rare earth concentrate as feed for the White Mesa separation plant.

Phase 1 capital cost is A$450M, largely covered by EFR's A$183M equity contribution and the A$200M debt package. EFR has invested A$60M for a 15.3% interest and needs about A$86M (US$60M) more plus US$14M of shares to reach 49%.
EFR ended Q2 2026 with about $937M in cash and marketable securities, which Canaccord says leaves it well funded for the remaining equity contribution.
